items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: California Bankers Association Bank Presidents Seminar (virtual): 'Modernizing Supervision and Regulation: 2025 and the Path Ahead'
items.quote: A simple solution would be to adjust thresholds by nominal GDP, which includes both economic growth and inflation.
items.summary: Supervision and regulation agenda (tailoring, thresholds, supervisory reform). No monetary-policy content in the prepared text.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Outlook 26: The New England Economic Forum, Foxborough: 'Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy'
items.quote: Absent a clear and sustained improvement in labor market conditions, we should remain ready to adjust policy to bring it closer to neutral.
items.summary: Sees policy as moderately restrictive, the labor market as increasingly fragile, and underlying inflation ex-tariffs close to 2 percent. Wants the Committee to keep focusing on employment risks, act preemptively, and avoid signaling a pause without evidence that conditions have changed.
items.score_note: Employment risks dominate and she argues against signaling a pause; she stops short of calling for a cut at the January meeting, so -1.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: American Institute for Economic Research / Shadow Open Market Committee / Florida Atlantic University conference, Boca Raton: 'Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy Implementation'
items.quote: the current policy stance leaves us well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate
items.summary: Cautiously optimistic: labor market stabilizing, inflation somewhat elevated, risks to both sides of the mandate. Says 175bp of cuts brought the funds rate into a range consistent with neutral and declines to prejudge the January meeting. Second half explains that reserve management purchases begun in December 2025 are not QE and have no implications for the policy stance.
items.score_note: Hold-and-watch language with two-sided risks; no lean either way.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Statement explaining his dissent at the January 27-28 FOMC meeting (the vote on January 28 was a hold; he preferred a 25bp cut)
items.quote: monetary policy is still restricting economic activity, and economic data make it clear to me further easing is needed
items.summary: Explains his January 28 dissent in favor of a 25bp cut. Labor market is weak (2025 payroll growth likely revised to zero), tariff inflation should be looked through, underlying inflation is close to 2 percent, and the policy rate is 50 to 75bp above neutral.
items.score_note: Dissent in favor of an immediate cut and says further easing is needed.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: SW Graduate School of Banking at SMU Cox, 161st Assembly for Bank Directors, Oahu: 'Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy'
items.quote: I continue to see policy as moderately restrictive, and, looking ahead to 2026, my Summary of Economic Projections includes three cuts for this year.
items.summary: Explains her vote to hold in January: after 75bp of cuts the Fed can 'keep policy powder dry' for a little while, with two more jobs and inflation reports before March. Downside labor risks have not diminished; the Fed should be ready to move toward neutral and should not imply an extended hold.
items.score_note: Voted to hold but projects three 2026 cuts and warns against signaling an extended pause; leaning easier, not calling for an immediate cut.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Economic Outlook and Supply-Side (Dis)Inflation Dynamics'
items.quote: The current policy stance is well positioned to address the risks to both sides of our dual mandate.
items.summary: Supported the January hold. Policy rate is broadly within the range of neutral estimates; further adjustments depend on data, outlook and balance of risks. Expects disinflation to resume once tariffs pass through; says AI-related demand could raise inflation temporarily but productivity gains leave more leeway without precautionary restraint. In the moderated Q&A (Brookings transcript PDF, https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/20260206_Transcript_unedited.pdf) he said the policy rate is supporting the labor market and he does not want to see any more weakening there, while inflation is still above target.
items.score_note: Explicitly balanced, meeting-by-meeting; the Q&A added nothing that tilts it.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: American Bankers Association 2026 Conference for Community Bankers, Orlando: 'Revitalizing Bank Mortgage Lending, One Step with Basel'
items.quote: These are legitimate concerns, and I want to be clear that holding MSRs is not the right choice for every bank.
items.summary: Bank capital treatment of mortgages and mortgage servicing rights. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta 2026 Banking Outlook Conference (pre-recorded video): Opening Remarks
items.quote: Last October, and for the first time, the Federal Reserve published supervisory operating principles.
items.summary: Opening remarks on the supervisory agenda, with a farewell to Atlanta Fed President Bostic. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: 42nd Annual NABE Economic Policy Conference, Washington: 'Labor Market Data: Signal or Noise?'
items.quote: As things stand today, I rate these two possible outcomes as close to a coin flip.
items.summary: After the strong January jobs report he says a March hold may be appropriate if February data confirm it, but if the good news is revised away a 25bp cut should be made in March; he rates the two outcomes a coin flip. Underlying inflation near 2 percent; the Supreme Court tariff ruling does not change his policy view. In Q&A (AP) he called solid growth with zero job growth something he had never seen.
items.score_note: Choice is only between holding and cutting, and he restates his January case for a cut; conditional rather than an outright call, so -1 not -2.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston 2026 Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference (via webcast): 'Operationalizing AI at the Federal Reserve'
items.quote: AI is one clear example of how the Federal Reserve can execute boldly, at scale, when we take a System-first approach.
items.summary: Speech on how the Federal Reserve System deploys AI tools internally. No statement on the rate path in the prepared text.
items.score_note: No monetary-policy content in the prepared text.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Testimony on Supervision and Regulation, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (prepared text)
items.quote: Therefore, I support efforts by Congress to reduce burden on community banks.
items.summary: Prepared testimony covers bank conditions, capital, supervision and community-bank relief. No statement on the rate path in the prepared text; the hearing Q&A was not reviewed.
items.score_note: Regulation only in the prepared text.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Roundtable on Liquidity and Lender of Last Resort, Committee on Capital Markets Regulation, Washington: 'Liquidity Resiliency, Financial Stability, and the Role of the Federal Reserve'
items.quote: Some see tension between monetary policy implementation tools and regulatory objectives.
items.summary: Discount window stigma and modernization and liquidity regulation. Touches the interaction of implementation tools with liquidity rules but says nothing on the rate path.
items.score_note: Liquidity regulation and discount window design only.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Fox Business interview on the day of the February jobs report (payrolls -92,000)
items.quote: This confirms to me that the labor market continues to be weak, and it could use some support from our policy rate.
items.summary: Says she was fine with the January hold, but the weak February jobs report suggests January strength may have been an anomaly and the labor market could use support from the policy rate. Bloomberg headlined it 'Labor Market May Need More Support'. Last remarks before the March blackout. The source page is dated March 7 and relays Bloomberg's report of the March 6 interview.
items.score_note: Clear easing lean on labor weakness; only one secondary page with the quote was readable (Bloomberg original is paywalled), so I kept -1 rather than -2.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Cato Institute Policy Forum on Basel III and Bank Capital Rules, Washington: 'Capital Rules for the Real Economy'
items.quote: Changes to the G-SIB surcharge based on underlying risk are appropriate but increases driven mainly by real economic growth and inflation do not reflect increases in systemic risk.
items.summary: Bank capital proposals (Basel III endgame, G-SIB surcharge, stress capital). No monetary-policy content. Delivered during the pre-FOMC blackout.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: CNBC 'Squawk Box' interview, two days after the March FOMC
items.quote: if things go reasonably well and the labor market continues to be weak, I would start advocating again for cutting the policy rate later this year
items.summary: Says caution is warranted after the Iran war and oil spike and that he voted to hold in March, but this does not mean staying put all year. Would resume advocating cuts later in 2026 if the labor market stays weak; also wants to see whether tariff effects roll off and what happens to inflation. Reuters reports he said he had planned to dissent for a cut after the February payroll loss until the Strait of Hormuz closure raised inflation risk.
items.score_note: Holds for now but the only direction he discusses is resuming cuts; torn between 0 and -1, kept -1 because the stated lean is explicitly toward easing later this year.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Fox Business 'Mornings with Maria' interview, two days after the March FOMC
items.quote: I've written three cuts in for before the end of 2026 to hopefully support the labor market.
items.summary: Still concerned about the job market and has three cuts in her 2026 projection, against a Committee median of one. Says it is too early to tell what longer-term imprint the Iran war will leave on activity and on rate decisions; expects strong growth supported by supply-side policies.
items.score_note: Projects three cuts this year to support jobs but had just voted to hold and names no timing; torn between -1 and -2, chose -1.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: Global Perspectives Speaker Series, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas: 'Economic Outlook and Energy Effects'
items.quote: I am confident that our current policy stance is well positioned to respond to a range of outcomes.
items.summary: Supported the March hold. Sees downside risk to the labor market and upside risk to inflation, with the energy price jump from the Middle East conflict and tariff uncertainty complicating both sides. Rate is broadly neutral; still speaks of 'additional adjustments' depending on data.
items.score_note: Two-sided risks named explicitly, stance described as well positioned; no lean.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: CBA LIVE 26, Consumer Bankers Association, San Diego: 'Supporting Small Businesses'
items.quote: Small businesses create and maintain the largest share of these new jobs.
items.summary: Small-business credit and the regulatory agenda. Mentions the dual mandate only in passing; no rate-path content.
items.score_note: Regulation and small-business lending only.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: College of Business Administration, University of Detroit Mercy: 'Economic Outlook and the Labor Market'
items.quote: I continue, however, to see our current policy stance as appropriately positioned to allow us to assess how the economy evolves.
items.summary: Repeats the March message: labor market roughly in balance but vulnerable, inflation above target, downside risk to jobs and upside risk to inflation. Supported the March hold; rate is broadly neutral and the stance allows time to assess energy-price and conflict effects.
items.score_note: Hold with two-sided risks; no lean.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: David Kaserman Memorial Lecture, Auburn University: 'One Transitory Shock After Another'
items.quote: leaving me cautious about rate cuts now and more inclined toward cuts to support the labor market later this year when the outlook is more steady
items.summary: Two scenarios. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens he can look through energy prices: cautious on cuts now, inclined to cut later this year. If energy stays elevated, inflation may become embedded and holding the rate at the current range may be needed if inflation risks outweigh labor risks. Warns that a sequence of shocks requires more vigilance on expectations.
items.score_note: Hold now with a conditional cut lean in one scenario and an inflation-driven hold in the other; torn between -1 and 0, chose 0.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Brookings Institution, Washington: 'Modernizing Federal Reserve Operations in the 21st Century'
items.quote: Each Bank president still has an independent voice at the FOMC on the appropriate course of monetary policy and that should continue.
items.summary: Speech on consolidating Reserve Bank back-office operations while keeping regional voices on the FOMC. No statement on the rate path. Delivered during the pre-FOMC blackout period.
items.score_note: Operations and governance only; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: FSOC Artificial Intelligence Series Roundtable on Cybersecurity and Risk Management, Washington: 'Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System'
items.quote: AI will become a force multiplier for the financial system, and in the broader U.S. economy.
items.summary: AI use in banks, supervisory approach and cyber risk. No monetary-policy or AI-financing content.
items.score_note: Supervision only.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: 2026 Women in Housing and Finance Symposium, Washington: 'A Coordinated Approach to Consumer Fraud Protection'
items.quote: One of the Federal Reserve's most important roles is to regulate banks and payments, and fraud poses a significant risk for both.
items.summary: Consumer fraud and payments scams. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Hoover Institution Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Stanford: 'Update On Federal Reserve Bank Operations'
items.quote: What I want to talk about is central bank independence but applied to Reserve Bank operations.
items.summary: Follow-up on Reserve Bank operational consolidation and independence. No statement on the rate path in the prepared text.
items.score_note: Operations only; no rate-path content.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Hoover Institution Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Stanford: 'When Regulation Reshapes Markets: The Migration of Corporate Lending'
items.quote: Instead of talking about monetary policy, my remarks will focus on this topic.
items.summary: Financial-stability speech on the migration of corporate lending to private credit funds and BDCs: BDC redemptions, bank lending to private credit vehicles, and a capital proposal to stop favoring loans to funds over direct corporate loans. Explicitly not about monetary policy. Notes worries about private-credit exposure to industries vulnerable to AI, such as software.
items.score_note: She states she is not discussing monetary policy; no rate-path content.
items.ai_quote: More recently, worries about exposures to industries vulnerable to the implementation of AI, such as the software sector, have compounded these concerns.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City 2026 Future of Banking Conference (pre-recorded video): Opening Remarks
items.quote: Since the global financial crisis, the regulatory and supervisory approaches designed for large institutions have often been pushed down to community banks.
items.summary: Opening remarks on community banking and supervision. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: Regulation only.

items.speaker: Christopher Waller
items.occasion: Centre for Central Banking Guest Lecture, Frankfurt School of Finance and Management: 'Policy Risks Have Changed'
items.quote: I can no longer rule out rate hikes further down the road if inflation does not abate soon
items.summary: Hawkish pivot. Inflation is 'not headed in the right direction'; he would remove the easing-bias language so a cut is no more likely than a hike, and would not hesitate to hike if expectations become unanchored. But hikes in the near future are premature and policy is still restrictive, so his position is to hold. Needs better inflation or a significant labor deterioration before considering cuts. In Q&A (Reuters) he called talk of near-term cuts 'kind of crazy'.
items.score_note: Inflation risk now dominates, pushes back on cut talk and opens the door to hikes, but explicitly says a hike now is premature, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Philip Jefferson
items.occasion: 2026 Bank of Japan-IMES Conference, Tokyo: 'Global Economic Developments and the U.S. Economy'
items.quote: I view risks around my inflation outlook as tilted to the upside
items.summary: Prepared text: inflation moved notably higher on energy costs, risks to his inflation outlook are tilted to the upside, labor-market risks somewhat to the downside; the current stance is well positioned and he has not prejudged June. Unlike his earlier 2026 speeches, the text no longer refers to the 'extent and timing of additional adjustments'. In the Q&A (Reuters, https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/feds-jefferson-says-he-focusing-inflation-us-labour-market-very) he said the labour market has been very resilient to the shock, so it seems appropriate that the focus be on returning inflation to 2%. Delivered the morning of May 28 Tokyo time (8:00 p.m. ET May 27 per the Board's speech listing).
items.score_note: The prepared text alone reads as a hold (0), but in the Q&A he said the focus should be on returning inflation to 2% given a resilient labour market, so inflation risk dominates: +1. No call for a hike. If only the official text is to count, use 0.

items.speaker: Michelle Bowman
items.occasion: Reykjavik Economic Conference 2026, Central Bank of Iceland: 'A Framework for Practical Monetary Policy Decision Making'
items.quote: Reacting to temporarily elevated energy price inflation would add unwarranted policy restraint, weighing unnecessarily on economic activity and labor market conditions.
items.summary: Lays out her conditions for cutting, hiking and holding. Calls policy moderately restrictive, supported keeping the statement's language on additional adjustments (the easing bias), and says it is appropriate to look through energy-driven inflation. But the longer the conflict and high oil prices persist, the more likely she will shift her view of the balance of risks. April core PCE 3.3 percent; ex one-offs only a bit above 2 percent.
items.score_note: Pushes back on tightening and defends the easing bias, which fits 'opposes further hikes'; the conditional hawkish caveat keeps it from -2.

coverage_notes: Sources: all 25 listed speech pages plus Bowman's Feb 26 testimony were opened on federalreserve.gov and each is an item (12 scored, 14 null incl. the testimony), plus 3 interview items from news pages with direct quotes (Waller CNBC Mar 20; Bowman Fox Business Mar 6 and Mar 20). The Board's speech and testimony feeds show no other entries for these three speakers in Jan-May 2026. time_et comes from the Board's speech listing feed (federalreserve.gov/json/ne-speeches.json), not from the speech pages themselves; interviews have null time (both Mar 20 interviews were reported by wires by about 9:00 a.m. ET). Dissents: FOMC statements for Jan 28, Mar 18 and Apr 29 were opened. Waller dissented only on Jan 28 (with Miran, for a 25bp cut); his explanatory statement of Jan 30 is the item, so there is no separate Jan 28 item because the FOMC statement has no words of his own. Waller voted with the majority in March and April; Jefferson and Bowman voted with the majority at all three meetings. April dissents were Miran (cut) and Hammack, Kashkari, Logan (against the easing bias), matching the brief. Bowman Mar 6: the only readable page with her quote is a secondary site (coingape, dated Mar 7) relaying Bloomberg's report of the Fox Business interview; the Bloomberg original is paywalled; the interview date (Friday Mar 6) was cross-checked on efn.se and the Bloomberg URL date. Jefferson May 27: scored +1 on the strength of Q&A remarks reported by Reuters (Kitco copy opened); the quote field is from the official text. Jefferson Feb 6 and Waller Apr 21 Q&As were read in the Brookings transcript PDFs (Waller's was in blackout with no policy content). Not included by rule (no rate-path content, not official speeches): Waller's Feb 24 Boston Fed Q&A (AI and jobs), Waller's May 31 panel in Croatia on stablecoins and CBDCs (PYMNTS relaying Bloomberg), Bowman's Apr 23 remarks on bank capital reported by Bloomberg. Not reviewed: Q&A portion of Bowman's Feb 26 Senate hearing; Q&A after Jefferson's Mar 26 and Apr 7 speeches and Bowman's Jan 30 fireside chat (wire headlines show only the prepared-text message); Waller's NABE Q&A beyond the AP report. Thin coverage: Waller in January (only the dissent statement; no pre-meeting remarks found) and Bowman in April (no monetary-policy remarks found; April 18-30 was blackout). Jefferson has exactly one policy occasion per month (none found beyond his official speeches). Discovery relied on the Board's feeds, Google News RSS headline scans by month, and a small number of web searches; Bloomberg, WSJ and Reuters originals were not readable, so interviews carried only by those outlets may be missing. Nothing I opened contradicts the context section of the brief.
